entities.summary:
The discovery of pulsars in 1967 by Jocelyn Bell Burnell and Antony Hewish at Cambridge University revolutionized astrophysics, providing the first observational evidence for neutron stars, a theoretical prediction since the 1930s. These celestial objects, initially dubbed "LGM-1" for "Little Green Men" due to their extraordinarily precise periodic radio signals, are rapidly rotating, highly magnetized remnants of massive stars that have undergone supernova explosions. Pulsars emit beams of electromagnetic radiation from their magnetic poles, which, when swept across Earth's line of sight like a cosmic lighthouse, create observable pulses ranging from milliseconds to seconds. This groundbreaking observation not only confirmed a major tenet of stellar evolution but also opened entirely new avenues in high-energy astrophysics, gravitational wave research, and fundamental physics. 

The serendipitous discovery occurred while Bell Burnell, then a postgraduate student, was analyzing data from a newly constructed radio telescope designed to study quasars. She meticulously identified an anomalous, highly regular signal that pulsed every 1.337 seconds, distinct from any known terrestrial or astronomical interference. Following months of rigorous verification and the identification of three more such objects, the team announced their findings, forever changing our understanding of extreme astrophysical phenomena. Subsequent observations confirmed pulsars as cosmic laboratories for testing general relativity, measuring gravitational wave effects, and even serving as highly stable cosmic clocks for deep-space navigation, demonstrating their profound utility beyond mere existence.
